clusters.text: Apple has updated the base 14-inch MacBook Pro and the iMac models with its latest generation M6 processor. The MacBook Pro was previously running the M5 chip from 2025 while the iMac was last updated in 2024 with the M4. The base 14-inch MacBook Pro model with the M6 processor gets a 12-core CPU with the 2+4+6 layout as well as a 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core and hardware accelerated ray tracing support. There's also a separate dual 16-core Neural Engine. The base configuration includes 16GB unified memory that can be configured to 24GB or 32GB. Only the latter two memory configurations get the full 170GB/s memory bandwidth, while the base 16GB option gets 153GB/s memory bandwidth. As for storage, you get 1TB as standard, with options for 2TB and 4TB being available. Aside from the M6, the 14-inch MacBook Pro also gets the new Apple N1 wireless networking chip, which upgrades the Wi-Fi to Wi-Fi7 802.11be, and Bluetooth 6. The iMac also gets the new M6 chip, but you get two configurations of it. The top model gets the same fully enabled chip mentioned above for the 14-inch MacBook Pro. However, the base iMac model gets a cut down version of the chip, which has a 10-core CPU in a 2+3+5 configuration, and a 10-core GPU with Neural Accelerators and ray tracing. Both models get the dual 16-core Neural Engine. Both iMac models get 16GB unified memory as standard, with options for 24GB for the base variant and 24GB or 32GB for the top variant. Interestingly, Apple does not claim different memory bandwidth numbers for the iMac, meaning even the 16GB model supposedly gets the full 170GB/s memory bandwidth. Both iMac models get 256GB SSD storage as standard, with options for 512GB or 1TB for both, and an additional 2TB option for the top model. Like the MacBook Pro, the iMac also gets the Apple N1 wireless networking chip. Finally, the iMac also gets option to add a nano texture to the display. Aside from these changes, both the 14-inch MacBook Pro and the iMac are otherwise identical to the models they replace. The 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $1,999. The iMac starts at $1,499 for the 10-core model and $1,699 for the 12-core model. Both computers will be up for pre-order tomorrow, October 28, and will be on sale Friday, November 6. clusters.text: Sale makes ‘Jodi’, a smaller relative of T rex, the ‘second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction’, Sotheby’s says A rare skeleton of a Nanotyrannus, a smaller relative of the Tyrannosaurus rex, sold at auction in New York this week for $47.3m, making it one of the world’s most expensive fossils. The skeleton, named “Jodi” after the person who found the remains in 2019, sold at Sotheby’s on Tuesday for $47.3m, “after a twelve-minute bidding battle that saw six bidders compete online and over the phones, before ultimately selling on the phone”, Sotheby’s said in a statement. Sotheby’s initially estimated that the skeleton would sell for $6m to $9m. Tuesday’s result makes “Jodi” the “second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction”, Sotheby’s noted. The buyer has not yet been identified publicly. The skeleton, which was unveiled at a Manhattan auction earlier this month, was discovered by Jodi Pierson in 2019 on her privately owned land in the Hell Creek Formation in Garfield County, Montana, near the town of Jordan. According to Sotheby’s, the skeleton measures 19.6ft long from nose to the tail, and around 9.6ft tall on the armature, “comprising approximately 191 fossil bone elements”. In a statement on Tuesday, Cassandra Hatton, vice-chair and worldwide head of science and natural history at Sotheby’s, thanked the team who assisted in the efforts to “excavate and save ‘Jodi’”. “Their passion and expertise have been fundamental to Jodi’s story,” Hatton said. “From the discovery and excavation, their commitment to understanding and preserving this remarkable specimen has helped bring us to this moment, a testament to the fact that we can all make major contributions to science. clusters.text: Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever developed, offering a remarkable new way to explore how the cosmos evolved after the Big Bang. Known as "Lumina," the simulation was built by researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian to help astronomers interpret observations from powerful instruments such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Nancy Roman Space Telescope. The research, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society , reconstructs the universe's first 2 billion years by modeling the interactions between ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation. By comparing Lumina's predictions with observations from JWST, Roman, and other telescopes, scientists can evaluate how well existing theories explain cosmic evolution and identify discoveries that might challenge their understanding of the universe's fundamental laws. Astronomers have spent centuries studying the sky and developing explanations for the formation of stars, galaxies, and other cosmic structures. Modern supercomputers now make it possible to turn these ideas into detailed simulations that predict how the universe should behave. When telescope observations agree with those predictions, they strengthen confidence in current theories. Unexpected differences, however, may point toward physical processes that scientists have yet to fully understand. "With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics," said lead author Oliver Zier, an ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. "To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video." Lumina is the largest cosmological radiation hydrodynamics simulation ever produced. In simple terms, it uses powerful computers to calculate how gas, dark matter, and light influenced one another as the young universe developed.
